feb/day-11/calocerus.summary: St. Calocerus, Bishop of Ravenna, who served as vicar and priest under St. Apollinaris, the city's first bishop, and later succeeded to the see under Emperor Hadrian. He is said to have converted nearly all the people of Ravenna and died a centenarian. The Bollandist commentary examines claims that he was a disciple of St. James in Spain.

feb/day-11/martyrs-felix.summary: A brief commentary on the African martyrs Felix, Victor, Januarius, Vitalis, and Herenaeus, recorded in the manuscript Martyrology of Reichenau and the Hieronymian Martyrology. They are tentatively connected to the group of confessors mentioned by Lucianus in a letter among the works of St. Cyprian, dating to around 250.

feb/day-11/martyrs-zoticus.summary: A short notice on the martyrs Zoticus, Cyriacus, Ammonius, Occominius, and Peleonicus, known from the Hieronymian and Reichenau martyrologies. Their place and circumstances of martyrdom are uncertain, and the commentary attempts to distinguish them from similarly named martyrs on adjacent days.

feb/day-11/basilius-in-armenia.summary: A brief notice on St. Basilius, a martyr in Armenia attested by the Hieronymian Martyrology and the Reichenau manuscript. His Acts are lost, and the commentary raises the question of whether he might be identical with the Basilius the monk venerated on February 12.

feb/day-11/martyrs-basilianus.summary: A short notice on the martyrs Basilianus, Amantius, and Tulicus in Campania and elsewhere, drawn from manuscript martyrologies of Liessies, Tournai, and the Hieronymian Martyrology. Their Acts are unknown.

feb/day-11/martyrs-of-apamea.summary: A brief commentary on the martyrs Poenes (or Poeon) and Euphraxius (or Eupraxius) at Apamea, attested in the Reichenau manuscript and Notker. The city Apamea could be any of several ancient cities of that name in Syria, Bithynia, Pisidia, or Gaul.

feb/day-11/simplides.summary: St. Simplides, eleventh Bishop of Vienne in Gaul, who flourished at the end of the third century under the emperors Tacitus, Probus, and Carus. Some sources honor him as a martyr; Ado recognized him only as a confessor. He completed the basilica of St. Peter begun by his predecessor.

feb/day-11/tigrinus.summary: St. Tigrinus, an early Roman martyr whose body was excavated from the cemetery of Priscilla on the Via Salaria under Pope Paul V and sent by the Jesuit Superior General Claudius Aquaviva to Turin in 1611, where it is venerated in the Jesuit church alongside relics of Theban Legion martyrs.

feb/day-11/martyrs-saturninus-the-priest.summary: The passio of Saturninus the Priest, Dativus the Lector, and some forty-seven companions arrested and martyred at Carthage in 303 during the Diocletianic persecution for gathering to celebrate the Lord's Supper in defiance of imperial edicts. This is one of the most detailed early African martyrdom accounts.

feb/day-11/martyrs-lucius-the-bishop-and.summary: St. Lucius, Bishop of Hadrianopolis in Thrace, and citizens of that city who refused communion with the Arians condemned at the Council of Sardica. Lucius was repeatedly exiled in chains and died in exile; his companions were beheaded by order of the Emperor Constantius through Count Philagrius in 348. The account draws on the testimony of St. Athanasius.

feb/day-11/jonas.summary: St. Jonas, a monk and gardener at the monastery of Muchonse in Egypt under the discipline of St. Pachomius. After eighty-five years in the monastery, he never tasted the fruit of the trees he planted. The vita, drawn from the Life of St. Pachomius, illustrates monastic obedience and ascetic self-denial.

feb/day-11/lazarus.summary: St. Lazarus, Bishop of Milan around the year 449, praised by St. Ennodius of Pavia in an epigram that describes his austere character and hidden labors during the Gothic invasions. Ennodius accorded him the title 'Saint' alongside only Ambrose and Simplicianus among Milan's bishops.

feb/day-11/castrensis.summary: St. Castrensis, an African bishop and confessor who was expelled from Africa during the Vandal persecution around 438-440 and set adrift on a decrepit ship with eleven companions. He reached the shores of Campania, settled near the mouth of the river Vulturnus, and propagated Christianity in the region until his death on February 11.

feb/day-11/secundinus.summary: St. Secundinus, a bishop whose body was discovered among the ruins of the ancient city of Aecana (now Troia) in Apulia during the construction of the new city around 1018-1022. Two accounts of the discovery survive: an anonymous contemporary history and a more literary version by Guaiferius, a Cassinese monk writing under Abbot Desiderius.

feb/day-11/euphrosyna.summary: St. Euphrosyna, a virgin of Alexandria who disguised herself as a male monk named Smaragdus and lived undetected in a monastery for twenty-eight (or thirty-eight) years, revealing her identity only on her deathbed. The commentary distinguishes her from St. Euphrasia of Constantinople and discusses the various feast days assigned to her.

feb/day-11/severinus.summary: St. Severinus, Abbot of Agaunum (Saint-Maurice in the Valais), who died in 506 at Chateau-Landon in Gaul. The commentary discusses the famous monastery at the site of the Theban Legion's martyrdom, its refounding by King Sigismund of Burgundy in 515 with perpetual choral psalmody, and Severinus's role in its earlier monastic life.

feb/day-11/ecianus.summary: St. Ecianus (or Echenus), Bishop of Cluainfoda in Ireland, active around 577. Born through the patronage of St. Brigid, he was renowned for miracles, including ploughing without a ploughshare and taming a wild stag to draw the plough. He ordained St. Columba to the priesthood rather than the episcopate.

feb/day-11/desideratus.summary: St. Desideratus, nineteenth Bishop of the Arverni (Clermont) in Gaul, who succeeded St. Avitus around the year 600. His body was translated from his own church to the basilica of St. Illidius after the former was destroyed. His Acts are unknown.

feb/day-11/caedmon.summary: St. Caedmon, a monk at Whitby (Streaneshealh) in Northumbria under Abbess St. Hilda, who around 670 received a miraculous gift of sacred song. His Life, drawn from Bede's Ecclesiastical History, tells how an unlettered herdsman was divinely inspired to compose vernacular hymns on Scripture, becoming one of the earliest known English-language poets.

feb/day-11/gaudinus.summary: St. Gaudinus, Bishop of Soissons and martyr around 720. He was seized and drowned in a well at the village of Herlin by usurers whom he had publicly rebuked. His relics were elevated on June 1 together with those of the bishops Principius and Lupus.

feb/day-11/theodora.summary: St. Theodora, Byzantine Empress, wife of Theophilus and mother of Michael III, who restored the veneration of sacred images after her husband's iconoclast reign. Born in Paphlagonia to pious parents, she secretly preserved icons during the persecution, and after Theophilus's death in 842 she convened a council that formally ended Iconoclasm. She was later expelled from the palace and forced into a monastery by her own son.

feb/day-11/ehoarnus.summary: St. Ehoarnus, a hermit at the monastery of St. Gildas de Rhuys in Brittany, murdered around 1020 by a robber named Leopardus who struck him with an axe on the threshold of the church. The killer was immediately seized by a demon and wandered naked and insane for twenty years, as attested by the author of the Life of St. Gildas who was an eyewitness.

feb/day-11/adolphus.summary: St. Adolphus, Bishop of Osnabruck in Westphalia (d. 1222), who converted from life as a Canon of Cologne Cathedral to Cistercian monasticism at Altenkamp after witnessing the monks' penitential discipline. He governed Osnabruck for twenty-one years, distinguished by his charity to lepers and miracles at his tomb.

feb/day-12/martyrs-of-brescia-valerianus.summary: A brief notice on the martyrs Valerianus, Valentinus, and Saprutius of Brescia, who suffered under Hadrian alongside SS. Faustinus and Jovita. Their discovery is celebrated on February 12, and their relics are preserved in the church of SS. Faustinus and Jovita ad Sanguinem.

feb/day-12/eulalia.summary: St. Eulalia, virgin martyr of Barcelona, who suffered at age fourteen on February 12, 303. The Bollandist commentary carefully distinguishes her from the more famous St. Eulalia of Merida (December 10), addressing the longstanding confusion between the two Spanish virgin martyrs who bore the same name and endured similar torments.

feb/day-12/martyrs-of-carthage.summary: A brief notice on the Carthaginian martyrs Modestus and Posinnus (or Posinna), attested in the Hieronymian Martyrology. The commentary addresses the erroneous addition of Julian to their company, who properly belongs among the Alexandrian martyrs.

feb/day-12/alexandrian-martyrs-julian.summary: A notice on a large group of Alexandrian martyrs including Julian, Victor, Felix, Secundus, Severian, Carpophorus, Germanus, Cyriacus, Ammonius, Euminius, and Pamphilus, drawn from the Hieronymian Martyrology and various manuscript sources.

feb/day-12/alexandrian-martyrs-modestus-.summary: A brief notice on the Alexandrian martyrs Modestus and Ammonius (described as infants), together with Zoticus, Cyriacus, and Simplicius, drawn from the Hieronymian Martyrology.

feb/day-12/damian.summary: St. Damian, a soldier and martyr in Africa (or possibly Alexandria), attested in Bede, Ado, Notker, and the Roman Martyrology. The Hieronymian Martyrology places him at Alexandria. His time and manner of martyrdom are unknown.

feb/day-12/italian-martyrs-donatus.summary: A brief notice on the Italian martyrs Donatus, Heradius (or Heraclius), Vincent, Susanna, Orbana, and Donata, attested in manuscript martyrologies.

feb/day-12/martyrs-macarius.summary: A commentary on the martyrs Macarius, Rufinus, and Justus at Seville in Spain, attested in manuscript martyrologies and the archiepiscopal archive of Seville. Their companion Peter is venerated separately on October 8.

feb/day-12/hippolytus.summary: St. Hippolytus, an early Roman martyr whose body was brought from Rome to the Benedictine monastery of the Holy Sepulchre at Cambrai in 1650. The translation on February 12, 1651, was celebrated with an elaborate procession, and Pope Innocent X granted a perpetual plenary indulgence for the feast.

feb/day-12/martyrs-saturninus-and-plutin.summary: A brief notice on the martyrs Saturninus and Plutinus, known from the Greek Menaea, who ended their lives by the sword. They are distinguished from the Carthaginian martyrs of the same period.

feb/day-12/florus.summary: St. Florus, an early Roman martyr whose body was excavated from the cemetery of St. Agnes on the Via Nomentana and brought to the Jesuit Professed House at Antwerp, where his annual celebration is observed on February 12.

feb/day-12/meletius-the-great.summary: St. Meletius the Great, Bishop of Antioch (d. 381), a champion of Nicene orthodoxy who was exiled three times by Arian emperors. Initially appointed to the see by the Arian party who expected him to share their views, he openly preached the consubstantiality of the Son and was immediately banished. He presided over the Second Ecumenical Council at Constantinople, where he died.

feb/day-12/gaudentius.summary: St. Gaudentius, Bishop of Verona, praised for his preaching and charity, who died on February 12. His body is preserved in an ancient marble chest in the church of St. Stephen at Verona, together with four other bishops.

feb/day-12/simplicius.summary: A notice on a Bishop Confessor named Simplicius, whose deposition is recorded in the most ancient martyrologies on February 12, though his identity is uncertain. He may be Simplicius of Verona, or possibly Simplicius of Bourges, the bishop whose election was famously announced by Sidonius Apollinaris.

feb/day-12/rioc.summary: St. Rioc, a fifth-century monk at Landevennec in Armorican Brittany and disciple of St. Winwaloe. He is chiefly remembered for raising his mother from the dead by sprinkling her with water blessed by his master and invoking Winwaloe's name.

feb/day-12/basil.summary: St. Basil, a monk of the island of Ratz in Gaul, attested in the ancient Martyrology of St. Savin in the Pyrenees and in Belgian manuscript martyrologies. The location of the island of Ratz is uncertain, possibly in Novempopulania near the river Ratus.

feb/day-12/constantius-at-brescia-in-ita.summary: St. Constantius, a count who abandoned military life after hearing the Gospel counsel of perfection, built a church dedicated to the Mother of God at Conche near Brescia along with twenty-four other churches. A dove miraculously indicated the foundations for his first church. His era is uncertain.

feb/day-12/ethelwold.summary: St. Ethelwold, Bishop of Lindisfarne (d. 740), who served as a minister of St. Cuthbert before becoming Provost, then Abbot of the monastery of Melrose in Scotland, and finally Bishop of the holy island of Lindisfarne in Northumbria.

feb/day-12/benedict.summary: St. Benedict of Aniane (d. 821), the great Carolingian monastic reformer who built the monastery of Aniane in the diocese of Maguelone in Narbonese Gaul and later the monastery of Inde (Kornelimunster) in Belgica. He was the chief architect of the monastic reform under Louis the Pious, establishing uniform observance of the Rule of St. Benedict across the Frankish Empire.

feb/day-12/antony-cauleas.summary: St. Antony Cauleas, Patriarch of Constantinople (d. 895), who served during the reign of Emperor Leo VI the Wise. Venerated by both Greeks and Latins, he succeeded St. Stephen (brother of Leo VI) and was celebrated for his pastoral holiness.

feb/day-12/goslinus.summary: St. Goslinus (or Goselinus), Abbot of the Benedictine monastery of St. Solutor near Turin, who died in holiness around 1061. His sacred body was discovered 411 years after his death, and his relics were eventually translated to the Jesuit church in Turin.

feb/day-12/ludanus.summary: St. Ludanus, a pilgrim venerated in Alsace between Strasbourg and Benfeld, who died in 1202. His relics are preserved in a parish church now called Saint Luden near the village of Hipsheim on the river Ill. A brief Life survives from the Canons Regular of Bodeken.

feb/day-12/alexius.summary: St. Alexius, Metropolitan of Kiev (d. c. 1364), one of the last orthodox prelates of Kiev in communion with Rome before the Greek-Russian schism prevailed. The commentary places him in the context of the Lithuanian conquest of Kiev under Gediminas and Olgerd.

feb/day-13/agabus-the-prophet.summary: St. Agabus, a first-century prophet mentioned in Acts 11:28 and 21:10-11, who foretold the great famine under Claudius and symbolically predicted St. Paul's arrest at Jerusalem. Venerated at Antioch in Syria, he is reckoned among the seventy disciples of Christ by the Greeks and is believed by some to have died a martyr.

feb/day-13/policetus.summary: St. Policetus, a deacon at Caravis near Caesaraugusta (Zaragoza) in Spain, martyred under Nero. Serving under Bishop Athanasius, the reputed first bishop of Caesaraugusta, he was imprisoned and killed by the sword. His Acts survive in an ancient hymn from the Breviary of St. Nabor in Lorraine.

feb/day-13/martyrs-fusca.summary: SS. Fusca, a young virgin, and Maura, her nurse, who were martyred at Ravenna in the third century under the Governor Quintianus during the Decian persecution. The commentary traces their veneration at Ravenna, Torcello, and Venice.

feb/day-13/polyeuctus.summary: St. Polyeuctus, a soldier martyred at Melitene in Armenia around 259, one of the most celebrated military martyrs of the East. His cult was widespread, with temples dedicated to him at Constantinople and elsewhere. His story inspired Corneille's tragedy Polyeucte.

feb/day-13/julian.summary: A commentary on the martyr Julian venerated on February 13, whose place of martyrdom is disputed. Some martyrologies assign him to Lyon, others to Nicomedia, and the Hieronymian Martyrology records a Juliana at Nicomedia on this day. The confusion may have arisen from misplaced punctuation in manuscript sources.

feb/day-13/martyrs-of-alexandria-tullian.summary: A brief notice on the Alexandrian martyrs Tullianus, Antius, Cyriacus, and Ammonius, drawn from the Hieronymian Martyrology. The commentary attempts to distinguish these from the numerous similarly named martyrs recorded on adjacent days at Alexandria.

feb/day-13/benignus.summary: St. Benignus, a priest martyred at Todi in Umbria under Diocletian, in the ancient city on the banks of the Tiber.

feb/day-13/palladius.summary: St. Palladius, an early Roman martyr whose body was excavated from the cemetery of St. Agnes at Rome and brought to the Jesuit Professed House at Antwerp in 1652, where his feast is celebrated on February 13.

feb/day-13/juliana.summary: St. Juliana, a fourth-century matron of Turin who translated the bodies of the Theban Legion martyrs Solutor, Adventor, and Octavius and built a memorial cell over them, which later became the nucleus of the distinguished Benedictine monastery of St. Solutor.

feb/day-13/domninus.summary: St. Domninus, the first Bishop of Digne in the Maritime Alps of Gaul, who came from Africa with St. Marcellinus (or Marcellus), Bishop of Embrun, to preach the Gospel in the region.

feb/day-13/castor.summary: St. Castor, a priest trained at the school of St. Maximin at Trier, who ministered at Caradunum (Karden) on the Moselle and at Koblenz in the Rhineland. He is patron of both places, and his relics are preserved in the ancient basilica of St. Castor at Koblenz.

feb/day-13/martinianus.summary: St. Martinianus, a hermit in Palestine around 400, whose Life was written by a contemporary author. After being tempted by a prostitute named Zoe, whom he converted to a life of penance at a Bethlehem monastery, he withdrew to a rock in the sea where he lived in solitude assisted by a pious sailor.

feb/day-13/guimerra.summary: St. Guimerra (or Gimier), the first Bishop of Carcassonne in Gallia Narbonensis, who served for a decade converting the people to Christianity. His body is preserved in the cathedral church of St. Nazarius. The date of his episcopate is unknown.

feb/day-13/modomnocus.summary: St. Modomnocus (or Dominic), Bishop of Ossory in Ireland in the sixth century, a disciple of St. David of Menevia in Wales. He is said to have brought bees from David's monastery to Ireland, earning the nickname 'patron of bees' in Irish tradition.

feb/day-13/stephen.summary: St. Stephen, Abbot at Rieti in the Sabine country in the sixth century, whose deeds were recorded by St. Gregory the Great. The vita draws on Gregory's accounts of monastic life in central Italy.

feb/day-13/ermenilda.summary: St. Ermenilda, Queen of Mercia and Abbess of Ely (d. c. 700), descended from the royal houses of Kent, the Franks, and the Burgundians. Married to King Wulfhere of Mercia, she later renounced royal life and entered the monastery at Ely, succeeding her mother-in-law as abbess.

feb/day-13/gregory-ii.summary: St. Gregory II, Pope (d. 731), who vigorously opposed the Iconoclasm of the Emperor Leo the Isaurian, supported the missions of St. Boniface to Germany, and defended papal independence from Byzantine imperial authority. Baronius judged that had his writings survived in full, he would be deemed no less than Gregory the Great.

feb/day-13/fulcran.summary: St. Fulcran, Bishop of Lodeve in Languedoc (d. 1006), secondary patron of the city after St. Genesius. His Life was composed by Bernard Gui, the Dominican inquisitor who later became Bishop of Lodeve, drawing on ancient acts.

feb/day-13/gilbert.summary: St. Gilbert (or Gislebert), Bishop of Meaux in France, who flourished around the year 1004. Praised by historians as a man of outstanding virtue and distinguished by miracles, his Life was published in a brilliant style.

feb/day-13/peter.summary: St. Peter, Bishop of Vercelli in Piedmont (d. c. 1010), who on pilgrimage to the Holy Land was captured by Saracens in Egypt and imprisoned. Freed through the agency of St. Boninus, he returned to his see and recruited Boninus to govern the abbey of St. Michael of Lucedio.

feb/day-14/valentine.summary: A Bollandist commentary on a St. Valentine, Bishop and Martyr, venerated at Baga and Toro in Spain, supposedly martyred under Trajan. The commentary examines the complex confusion among several saints named Valentine on this day and the tendency of Spanish hagiographers to attribute to their local saints the deeds of the Italian Valentine of Terni.

feb/day-14/zeno.summary: St. Zeno, an early Roman martyr whose body was given to the Benedictine nuns of St. Margaret at Bologna in 1623 by Pope Gregory XV. The commentary also discusses several martyrs of the Via Flaminia recorded in the Hieronymian Martyrology.

feb/day-14/martyrs-ammon.summary: A brief notice on the martyrs Ammon, Jonas, Sammon, Stoppius, Protidius, Praeconidius, and Moses, attested in manuscript martyrologies.

feb/day-14/eleuchadius.summary: St. Eleuchadius, Bishop of Ravenna (d. c. 112), a philosopher converted by St. Apollinaris who made him a deacon. He eventually succeeded to the see of Ravenna and governed the church in the time of the emperors Trajan and Hadrian.

feb/day-14/alexandrian-martyrs-bassus.summary: A historical digest on a large group of Alexandrian martyrs including Bassus, Antonius, Protolycus, Cyrion the Priest, Bassianus the Lector, Agatho the Exorcist, Moses, Dionysius, Ammonius, and others, attested in manuscript martyrologies.

feb/day-14/alexandrian-martyrs-saturninu.summary: A brief notice on the Alexandrian martyrs Saturninus, Advotus, Praecunus, and Maximus, recorded in the Hieronymian Martyrology. Advotus and Praecunus are otherwise unknown in hagiographic literature.

feb/day-14/valentine-i.summary: St. Valentine I, Bishop of Terni (Interamna) in Umbria, martyred around 273. Ordained bishop by St. Felician of Foligno at the request of the people around 203, he is one of the most celebrated saints of February 14. The commentary carefully distinguishes him from the Roman priest Valentine and from a later Valentine III of Terni.

feb/day-14/martyrs-of-avellino-modestinu.summary: SS. Modestinus the Bishop, Florentinus the Priest, and Flavian the Deacon, martyrs at Avellino in Campania.

feb/day-14/maro.summary: St. Maro, an anchorite near Cyrrhus in Syria around 370, from whom the Maronite community takes its name. His life of austere asceticism on an open hilltop, without shelter from the elements, was recorded by Theodoret of Cyrrhus.

feb/day-14/abraames.summary: St. Abraames, Bishop of Carrhae (Harran) in Mesopotamia around 390, whose pastoral labors in a deeply pagan city were recorded by Theodoret of Cyrrhus.

feb/day-14/auxentius.summary: St. Auxentius, priest and archimandrite in Bithynia (d. c. 470), a noted ascetic who lived on a mountain near Chalcedon and was involved in the theological controversies surrounding the Council of Chalcedon.

feb/day-14/theodosius.summary: St. Theodosius, Bishop of Vaison in Gaul, who died around 554. Vaison, in Provence, was an ancient episcopal city where two important councils were held in the fifth and sixth centuries.

feb/day-14/martyrs-bruno.summary: St. Bruno, Archbishop and missionary to the pagan Prussians, martyred in 1008 with eighteen companions while preaching the Gospel on the borders of Prussia and Lithuania.

feb/day-15/brothers-faustinus.summary: SS. Faustinus the Priest and Jovita the Deacon, brothers and martyrs at Brescia in Italy, who suffered under Hadrian around 120. Among the most celebrated patron saints of Brescia, their cult is supported by ancient Acts and extensive local tradition.

feb/day-15/martyrs-joseph-the-deacon.summary: A notice on the martyrs Joseph the Deacon, Zeno, Apollonius, Phoebus, Romanus, Zosimus, Barolus, Zocus the Priest, and Rufinus at Antioch in Syria.

feb/day-15/crato-the-orator.summary: St. Crato, a Roman orator martyred around 273 with his wife and household, whose conversion is narrated in connection with the Acts of St. Valentine.

feb/day-15/agape.summary: St. Agape, a virgin martyr at Terni in Umbria around 273, whose martyrdom is connected with the persecution that also claimed St. Valentine of Terni.

feb/day-15/syrian-martyrs-adventus.summary: A notice on the Syrian martyrs Adventus, Xystus, Pomponius, Gemella, Victor, Generosus, Victor, Gemellianus, Cuturnus, and Castula, attested in manuscript martyrologies.

feb/day-15/faustina.summary: St. Faustina, a virgin martyr of uncertain date and place, known from manuscript martyrologies.

feb/day-15/eusebius.summary: St. Eusebius, an anchorite at Asicha in Syria after the year 400, whose ascetic life is recorded in the hagiographic traditions of the Syrian Desert Fathers.

feb/day-15/georgia.summary: St. Georgia, a virgin devoted to God at Clermont in Gaul, venerated for her holiness of life.

feb/day-15/severus.summary: St. Severus, a priest in Valeria (the region around the ancient Marsian territory in central Italy), who died around 530. His deeds were recorded by St. Gregory the Great in the Dialogues.

feb/day-15/quinidius.summary: St. Quinidius, Bishop of Vaison in Gaul (d. c. 578), successor in a see notable for its councils. He governed the church in Provence during the Merovingian period.

feb/day-15/berachius.summary: St. Berachius (or Berachus), an abbot and bishop in Ireland around the year 500, belonging to the early golden age of Irish monasticism.

feb/day-15/faustus.summary: St. Faustus, a Cassinese monk who died at Rome around 507, whose life is connected with the early Benedictine tradition at Monte Cassino.

feb/day-15/decorosus.summary: St. Decorosus, Bishop of Capua in Campania (d. c. 690), who governed his see during the Lombard period in southern Italy.

feb/day-15/walfrid.summary: St. Walfrid, Abbot of the monastery of Monteverde (Palazzuolo) in Etruria (d. c. 765), founder of a monastic community in Tuscany.

feb/day-15/columbanus.summary: St. Columbanus, abbot and recluse at Ghent in Flanders (d. 959), not to be confused with the more famous Columbanus of Bobbio. He lived as an enclosed monk in the Flemish city.

feb/day-15/sigfrid.summary: St. Sigfrid, Bishop and Confessor at Vaxjo in Sweden (d. c. 1045), an English missionary who brought Christianity to southern Sweden. His three nephews Vinamannus, Unamannus, and Sunamannus, who assisted in his mission, were martyred by pagans.

feb/day-15/martyrs-henry-and-alfard.summary: SS. Henry and Alfard, martyrs in Sweden and Norway around 1055, who fell in the course of the Christianization of Scandinavia.

feb/day-15/euseus.summary: St. Euseus (or Euseius), a hermit and cobbler at Serravalle in Piedmont, who combined manual labor with contemplative solitude.

feb/day-16/onesimus-the-apostle.summary: St. Onesimus, the fugitive slave of Philemon converted by St. Paul during his Roman imprisonment around AD 58, on whose behalf Paul wrote the Epistle to Philemon. He is said to have become Bishop of Ephesus and was martyred in 109. The Greeks count him among the Seventy Apostles.

feb/day-16/simeon.summary: St. Simeon, an early Bishop of Metz in Gaul in the second century, belonging to the apostolic succession of that ancient see.

feb/day-16/honestus.summary: St. Honestus, a priest and martyr around 270 who evangelized the people of Pamplona in Navarre, earning the title 'Apostle of the Pamplonians.'

feb/day-16/martyrs-proculus.summary: SS. Proculus, Ephebus, and Apollonius, martyrs at Interamna (Terni) in Umbria around 273, connected with the wider persecution that produced the martyrdom of St. Valentine of Terni.

feb/day-16/cornelius.summary: St. Cornelius, an early Roman martyr whose body was brought from Rome to the city of Ghent in Belgium.

feb/day-16/martyrs-julian-the-bishop.summary: SS. Julian the Bishop, John the Deacon, and five thousand companions, martyred in Egypt. The scale of the reported martyrdom reflects the severity of the persecutions in the Egyptian provinces.

feb/day-16/martyrs-elias.summary: SS. Elias, Jeremias, Esaias, Samuel, and Daniel, five Egyptian Christians martyred in 308 at Caesarea in Palestine during the Great Persecution, together with Porphyrius (servant of St. Pamphilus) and Seleucus of Cappadocia. Their martyrdom is recorded by Eusebius of Caesarea as an eyewitness.

feb/day-16/martyrs-plesius.summary: A notice on a group of eighteen martyrs including Plesius, Dionysius, Hierapius, Martialis, and others, attested in manuscript martyrologies. Their place and date of martyrdom are uncertain.

feb/day-16/faustinianus-and-iuventia.summary: SS. Faustinianus and Iuventia, martyrs in Britain, of whom very little is known beyond their names in the martyrological tradition.

feb/day-16/juliana.summary: St. Juliana, a virgin of Nicomedia martyred under Maximian, one of the most widely venerated female martyrs of the early Church. Her relics were translated to various locations, and she is particularly honored at Brussels. Her Acts describe her confrontation with the devil in prison.

feb/day-16/martyrs-of-nicomedia-five-hun.summary: Five hundred men and one hundred and thirty women martyred at Nicomedia under Maximian, reflecting the intense persecution in the imperial capital of the Eastern Empire during the Great Persecution.

feb/day-16/faustinus.summary: St. Faustinus, Bishop of Brescia in Italy around 370, a shepherd of his flock during the Arian controversies that convulsed the fourth-century Church in northern Italy.

feb/day-16/flavianus.summary: St. Flavianus, an anchorite in the East, known from hagiographic tradition as a practitioner of the ascetic life.

feb/day-16/tigridius.summary: St. Tigridius, a priest at Clermont in Gaul around 390, belonging to the early episcopal history of the Auvergne.

feb/day-16/tetradius.summary: St. Tetradius, a bishop of uncertain see, known only from the martyrological tradition.

feb/day-16/eulalius.summary: St. Eulalius, Bishop of Syracuse in Sicily, who died after 503. He governed the ancient see of Syracuse during the Ostrogothic period in Italy.

feb/day-16/tanco.summary: St. Tanco, Bishop of Verden in Lower Saxony around the year 800, who served as bishop during the Carolingian period of Saxon Christianization.

feb/day-17/mariamne.summary: St. Mariamne, identified as the sister of St. Philip the Apostle, an apostolic virgin of the first century who is said to have accompanied her brother in his missionary journeys and preached the Gospel in the East.

feb/day-17/polychronius.summary: St. Polychronius, Bishop of Babylon and martyr (d. 251), who was killed during the Decian persecution. His see at Babylon reflects the survival of Christian communities in Mesopotamia from very early times.

feb/day-17/martyrs-saturninus.summary: SS. Saturninus, Castulus (or Castula), Magnus, Lucius, Rogatus, John, and various companions, martyred at Interamna (Terni) in Umbria around 273, forming part of the extensive martyrological tradition of that city.

feb/day-17/eusebius.summary: St. Eusebius, an early Roman martyr whose body was brought from Rome to Ghent in Belgium, where it is venerated.

feb/day-17/martyrs-donatus.summary: SS. Donatus, Secundianus, Romulus, and about eighty companions, martyred at Concordia in northeastern Italy in 303 during the Diocletianic persecution.

feb/day-17/chrysanthianus-and-90-compani.summary: St. Chrysanthianus and ninety companion martyrs at Aquileia in northeastern Italy, part of the severe persecution in the region of Venetia during the Roman persecutions.

feb/day-17/faustinus-and-44-companion-ma.summary: St. Faustinus and forty-four companion martyrs, known from manuscript martyrologies. Their place and date of martyrdom are uncertain.

feb/day-17/bonosius.summary: St. Bonosius (or Bonosus), Bishop of Trier in Belgica Prima (d. 381), who governed the important metropolitan see during the period of the Arian controversies.

feb/day-17/pulchronius.summary: St. Pulchronius, Bishop of Verdun in Belgica Prima around 470, who shepherded his diocese during the turbulent final decades of the Western Roman Empire.

feb/day-17/bishops-lomanus-and-fortchern.summary: SS. Lomanus and Fortchernus, bishops at Trim in Meath, Ireland, in the fifth century, belonging to the first generation of the Patrician mission that established Christianity in Ireland.

feb/day-17/habetdeus.summary: St. Habetdeus, Bishop of Luna (modern Luni) in Liguria and martyr around 500, whose unusual Latin name means 'he has God.'

feb/day-17/fintan.summary: St. Fintan, priest and abbot of Cluain-Ednech (Clonenagh) in Ireland in the sixth century, a prominent figure of early Irish monasticism noted for his strict ascetic discipline.

feb/day-17/finan.summary: St. Finan, Bishop of Lindisfarne in Northumbria (d. 661), an Irish monk from Iona who succeeded St. Aidan and continued the evangelization of the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms, baptizing the Kings of the East Saxons and Mercians.

feb/day-17/silvinus.summary: St. Silvinus, a missionary bishop at Auchy in Belgica Secunda around 720, who evangelized the region of Therouanne and worked to free captives and baptize pagans in the Merovingian period.

feb/day-17/fulrad.summary: St. Fulrad, Abbot of Saint-Denis and Chief Chaplain (archicapellanus) of the Carolingian royal palace (d. 784). He served as a trusted diplomat and advisor to Pepin the Short and Charlemagne, playing a key role in securing papal recognition of the Carolingian dynasty.

feb/day-17/benedict.summary: St. Benedict, a bishop in Sardinia around the year 1100, of whom few details survive beyond the notice in manuscript sources.

feb/day-17/constabilis.summary: St. Constabilis, Abbot of the Benedictine monastery of Cava dei Tirreni in southern Italy (d. 1124), who continued the spiritual legacy of the great Cava abbots in the Norman period.

feb/day-18/simeon.summary: St. Simeon, second Bishop of Jerusalem and martyr, crucified in 107 under Trajan at the age of 120. A kinsman of Christ through Clopas, he was elected bishop by the apostles and disciples after the martyrdom of St. James, and governed the Jerusalem church through the destruction of the city in AD 70.

feb/day-18/martyrs-of-leontini-in-sicily.summary: A notice on anonymous early martyrs at Leontini (modern Lentini) in Sicily, who suffered around 255 during the persecutions of the mid-third century.

feb/day-18/leo-and-paregorius.summary: SS. Leo and Paregorius, martyrs at Patara in Lycia (southwestern Asia Minor), whose passio records their suffering during the Roman persecutions in the province known for its connection to St. Nicholas.

feb/day-18/roman-martyrs-maximus.summary: SS. Maximus, Count of the Privy Purse, his brother Claudius of senatorial rank, Claudius's wife Praepedigna, and their children Alexander and Cutia, Roman martyrs in 295. Their high social standing illustrates the penetration of Christianity into the Roman aristocracy before the Great Persecution.

feb/day-18/epimeneus.summary: St. Epimeneus (or Pimenius), a priest and martyr at Brescia in northern Italy, attested in local hagiographic traditions.

feb/day-18/african-martyrs-lucius.summary: A notice on the African martyrs Lucius, Silvanus, Rutulus, Classicus, Secundinus, Maximus, Fructulus, Damasus, Paulus, and Martialis, drawn from manuscript martyrologies.

feb/day-18/martyrs-marcellus.summary: A brief notice on the martyrs Marcellus, Macrobius, Geminus, Romulus, Silvina, Carsicius, and Fructulus, known from manuscript martyrologies. Their place and era are uncertain.

feb/day-18/legontius.summary: St. Legontius, Bishop of Metz in Belgica Prima around 325, belonging to the early succession of bishops in one of the most ancient sees of Gaul.

feb/day-18/roman-virgins-constantia-augu.summary: SS. Constantia Augusta, daughter of Constantine the Great, and Attica and Artemia, daughters of the consul St. Gallicanus, Roman virgins of the fourth century who devoted themselves to the service of God. Constantia is credited with building the basilica on the Via Nomentana in Rome that still bears her name.

feb/day-18/flavian.summary: St. Flavian, Bishop of Constantinople (d. 449), who was fatally beaten at the so-called 'Robber Council' of Ephesus for defending Christological orthodoxy against the Monophysite Eutyches and the imperial faction of Dioscorus of Alexandria. His cause was vindicated at the Council of Chalcedon in 451.

feb/day-18/helladius.summary: St. Helladius, Archbishop of Toledo in Spain (d. 632), who converted from high public office to the monastic life and was elected to the primatial see. He was a patron of learning in Visigothic Spain.

feb/day-18/culanus.summary: St. Culanus, a bishop in Ireland of uncertain date, known from Irish martyrological sources.

feb/day-18/colman.summary: St. Colman, Bishop of Lindisfarne (d. 676), an Irish monk who defended the Celtic observance of Easter at the Synod of Whitby in 664. After the ruling went against him, he resigned his see and withdrew with his monks first to Iona and then to Inishbofin off the coast of Ireland.

feb/day-18/angilbert.summary: St. Angilbert, Abbot of Centula (Saint-Riquier) in Picardy (d. 814), a Carolingian courtier, poet, and counselor of Charlemagne who became a monk and rebuilt the abbey of Centula into one of the great monasteries of the Empire.

feb/day-18/theotonius.summary: St. Theotonius, first Prior of the Canons Regular of the Holy Cross at Coimbra in Portugal (d. 1166), a key figure in the spiritual life of the nascent Portuguese kingdom. He was noted for his preaching, his pilgrimages to Jerusalem, and his friendship with Afonso Henriques, the first King of Portugal.

feb/day-19/auxibius.summary: St. Auxibius, Bishop of Soli in Cyprus (d. c. 102), said to have been ordained by St. Mark the Evangelist and to have governed his see for fifty years during the apostolic age.

feb/day-19/gabinius.summary: St. Gabinius, a Roman priest and martyr in 296, father of St. Susanna and brother of Pope St. Caius. He was martyred during the Diocletianic persecution.

feb/day-19/zambdas.summary: St. Zambdas (or Zabdas), Bishop of Jerusalem (d. 304), who governed the Holy City's church during the Great Persecution under Diocletian.

feb/day-19/legontius.summary: St. Legontius, Bishop of Trier in Belgica Prima around 409, who shepherded his flock during the traumatic period of barbarian invasions across the Rhine.

feb/day-19/odranus.summary: St. Odranus, a fifth-century Irish martyr who served as charioteer to St. Patrick. He was killed in Patrick's place, accepting a blow intended for the Apostle of Ireland.

feb/day-19/martyrs-in-palestine-under-al.summary: Anonymous Christian martyrs killed in Palestine in the sixth century by Alamundarus (al-Mundhir), a Saracen (Lakhmid Arab) chieftain allied with Persia, during his raids against the Roman frontier provinces.

feb/day-19/rabulas.summary: St. Rabulas, an abbot in the East around 530, known from Eastern hagiographic traditions. He is distinct from the famous Rabbula, Bishop of Edessa (d. 435).

feb/day-19/conon.summary: St. Conon, a priest and abbot of the monastery of Penthuclae in Palestine around 555, whose deeds are recorded in the traditions of Palestinian monasticism.

feb/day-19/mansuetus.summary: St. Mansuetus, Bishop of Milan in Italy, who died after 680. He presided over the see of Milan during the Lombard period and was involved in the theological controversies of the seventh century.

feb/day-19/barbatus.summary: St. Barbatus, Bishop of Benevento in southern Italy (d. 682), who converted the Lombards of Benevento from their remaining pagan practices, including the veneration of a sacred tree and a golden viper. He attended the Third Council of Constantinople in 680-681.

feb/day-19/beatus.summary: St. Beatus, a priest at Vallecava (Liebana) in Asturias, Spain (d. 798), celebrated for his Commentary on the Apocalypse and his vigorous opposition to the Adoptionist heresy promoted by Elipandus, Archbishop of Toledo.

feb/day-20/martyrs-of-tyre-tyrannio-the-.summary: St. Tyrannio, Bishop of Tyre in Phoenicia, and numerous companions who suffered martyrdom in 304 and 310 during the Great Persecution. Their sufferings are recorded by Eusebius of Caesarea, who was an eyewitness to the persecution in Tyre and Palestine.

feb/day-20/martyrs-potamius.summary: SS. Potamius, Nemesius, and Didymus, martyrs on the island of Cyprus, known from manuscript martyrologies.

feb/day-20/paula.summary: St. Paula, surnamed Barbata, a virgin of Avila in Spain who was martyred for refusing a pagan suitor during the Roman persecutions under the Governor Dacian. Her story is preserved in an ancient verse account.

feb/day-20/martyrs-sadoth-the-bishop-and.summary: St. Sadoth, Bishop of Seleucia-Ctesiphon in Persia, and 128 companions martyred in 345 during the great persecution under King Shapur II. Sadoth succeeded the martyred Catholicos Simeon bar Sabbae and was himself arrested and beheaded after months of imprisonment. This is one of the principal texts of the Syriac Acts of the Persian Martyrs.

feb/day-20/bishops-of-maastricht.summary: SS. Eucherius and Falco, bishops of Maastricht (Trajectum ad Mosam) in Belgium around the year 1000, venerated in the ancient episcopal tradition of that city on the Meuse.

feb/day-20/olcanus.summary: St. Olcanus (or Bolcanus), a bishop in Ireland around the year 1000, known from Irish martyrological sources.

feb/day-20/eleutherius.summary: St. Eleutherius, Bishop of Tournai in Belgium (d. 531), a major figure in the Christianization of the Belgic provinces. He converted much of the population from paganism and Arianism and was attacked and left for dead by Arian heretics.

feb/day-20/eucherius.summary: St. Eucherius, Bishop of Orleans (d. 743), who was exiled by Charles Martel for opposing the confiscation of church property. He died in exile at Saint-Trond (Sint-Truiden) in Belgium, a victim of the conflict between the Carolingian mayors of the palace and the Frankish episcopate.

feb/day-20/leo-the-wonderworker.summary: St. Leo the Wonderworker, Bishop of Catania in Sicily (d. c. 780), renowned for his miracles and his confrontation with the sorcerer Heliodorus. His Life is an important text for understanding popular religion and episcopal authority in Byzantine Sicily.
